segments.text: This resource expands the original Group IV Easy Crash Course chapter on British History into a fuller teaching text, preserving every preparation checklist, “common confusion,” and “easy revision point” from the original notes while adding background, fuller explanation, key terms, and a closing “Key Takeaways” section to each topic.

items.text: I. The Glorious Revolution (1688):
causes and results; William and Mary; Queen Anne.
II. The Hanoverian Era:
Jacobite rebellions; Walpole and Whig oligarchy; American War of Independence.
III. Union of England and Scotland.
IV. Union of England and Ireland.
V. The Old Colonial System.
VI. French Revolution and Napoleonic Wars:
causes, Britain’s role and effects on Britain.
VII. Industrial and Agricultural Revolutions:
causes and political/social effects; party politics; Methodist movement; socialism; liberalism; colonization; Chartism.
VIII. Robert Peel and Return of the Tories:
internal policies and the Irish problem.
IX. Victorian Era:
internal reforms, Liberals, foreign policy, Disraeli and Gladstone, Ireland and free trade.
X. Edwardian Era:
domestic and foreign policy; origins and development of the Labour Party.
XI. Britain in the First World War and Aftermath:
causes, peace settlement, League of Nations, Great Depression, appeasement and rearmament.
XII. Britain in the Second World War and Aftermath:
causes and events, Churchill, wartime conferences, United Nations, effects and Labour reforms.
XIII. Britain and the Cold War:
Commonwealth, NATO, decolonization, EEC, internal and foreign policy.
XIV. Thatcherism to Cameron (1979–2012):
domestic change, society, foreign policy, Falklands, Major, Europe, Blair/New Labour, War on Terror, 2008 crisis and Cameron reforms.
Build one timeline from 1688 to 2012, marking constitutional change, party development, industrialisation, empire and major wars in separate columns.
Reward continuity and change explicitly: ask what changed in Crown-Parliament relations, voting, parties, economy, empire and welfare after every major event.
Study prime ministers through policies and historical significance rather than personal biography.
Keep domestic and foreign policy connected: war, empire and economic change repeatedly produced major internal political reform.
When discussing Ireland, Scotland and empire, avoid writing only from Westminster’s perspective; include local political reactions and consequences.
Use comparison tables for Gladstone–Disraeli, Thatcher–Blair, and pre/post-war Britain.

intro.text: Final Revision Strategy for This Subject

segments.text: For every topic in this subject, build a short timeline, identify continuity and change explicitly (what changed in Crown-Parliament relations, party structure, franchise, empire or welfare), connect domestic and foreign policy wherever a war or imperial event is involved, and close with a comparison table wherever two leaders, parties, or periods are being contrasted (Gladstone–Disraeli, Thatcher–Blair, pre/post-war Britain).

items.text: Norman Lowe, Mastering Modern World History — a widely used survey covering nineteenth- and twentieth-century British and world history.
Standard British history surveys covering the Georgian, Victorian, and twentieth-century periods should be checked for edition and period coverage before use.

segments.text: Dates and institutional facts in this resource have been presented conservatively. Where historical interpretation is genuinely disputed (for instance, the precise weighting of causes behind British industrialisation, or the fairness of famine-era Irish policy), this resource aims to present the balance of evidence rather than a single simplified verdict.
